heroHeadline: Trump-Xi Beijing Summit Opens — US Clears H200 Chips for 10 Chinese Firms; Bessent Announces US-China AI Safety Dialogue; China Refuses to Buy, Steering to Huawei Ascend
heroSubtitle: The Trump-Xi Beijing summit opened May 14 at the Great Hall of the People — the first US presidential state visit to China since 2017 — with an unprecedented tech CEO delegation: Elon Musk (xAI/Tesla), Tim Cook (Apple), Larry Fink (BlackRock), and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang (last-minute addition, joined Trump in Alaska on May 13). The summit produced two immediate tech announcements: (1) Treasury Secretary Bessent told CNBC on May 14 that 'we are in the lead in AI' and that the US and China will begin formal talks on AI guardrails, best practices, and governance — the first institutionalized US-China AI safety dialogue under the Trump administration; (2) Xi Jinping met the tech CEO delegation and pledged China would 'open wider' to foreign business in AI and technology. In parallel, US Commerce cleared Nvidia H200 chip sales for approximately 10 Chinese firms including Alibaba, Tencent, ByteDance, and JD.com — but no orders have been placed. Beijing is actively directing domestic firms toward Huawei Ascend chips rather than purchasing Nvidia hardware, even when licenses are available: ByteDance ($5.6B Huawei Ascend order, April 2026), DeepSeek V4 running natively on Huawei Ascend 950PR (April 24), and Huawei's ~60% domestic AI chip market share all represent demand Beijing intends to capture domestically. China's SAMR suspended antitrust probes into Nvidia, Qualcomm, and Intel — signaling Beijing is wielding regulatory leverage rather than market purchasing as its primary chip diplomacy tool. The summit backdrop: the May 12 US-China trade truce reduced US tariffs on Chinese goods from ~145% to 30% (China's tariff on US goods fell from 125% to 10%), and Alibaba posted its first operating loss since the 2021 crackdown on May 13, signaling that Chinese Big Tech is prioritizing AI investment over near-term profitability. Xi opened with a warning that mishandling Taiwan would put the relationship in 'great jeopardy.' The core tech paradox of the summit: the US is offering chip access China is refusing to take, while China's domestic AI stack — Huawei Ascend hardware (60% domestic AI chip share, $12B 2026F revenue), DeepSeek/Doubao/Kimi models ($45B/$120T tokens/$20B), and Alibaba's loss-absorbing AI buildout — accelerates on every layer simultaneously.
